the main contribution of the present paper is to show that a computationally efficient algorithm can be designed to achieve Stackelberg regret, which is a type of policy regret, in the online linear classification problem with strategic agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we give a general framework for learning in a strategic setting, where agents can adaptively manipulate their features to respond to the learner, and we show how this framework can be used to obtain a variety of interesting learning results in the context of strategic classification.
we provide the first efficient algorithm for learning from strategic agents in the presence of strategic classification.

we show that it is possible to obtain a “Stackelberg equilibrium” in a strategic classification game, in the sense that the learner’s classifier is nearly as good as the best classifier in the game, even though agents are able to strategically manipulate their revealed preferences.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the learner is able to learn a classifier that is nearly as good as the best one in hindsight, even in the face of agents who have no incentive to reveal their true features, and are instead incentivized to manipulate their feature vectors to best respond to the learner’s classifier.
, even in the presence of adversarially chosen agents who are able to manipulate the data, the data still contains information about the underlying “true” features.
